questions.question: Write a design brief for the headgear in problem form, identify where each element comes from, and explain what the 'what we know' paragraph carries forward and why the brief is checked against the tender notice.
questions.expected_answer: A platinum mining company sinking a vertical shaft to a reef about 800 metres down near Rustenburg needs a headgear to support a wire-rope winding system that raises and lowers a cage of workers and a skip of ore safely and reliably, with the winder house 40 metres from the shaft; design the structure with its winding mechanism, demonstrate it as a working scale model that lifts a load up a model shaft, and cost the full-size structure. The need, users, setting and purpose come from the tender notice and the scenario, and the brief leaves the form open, naming no A-frame or gear count. The 'what we know' paragraph carries the structural forms and back-leg function and legal safety features from the investigation, the motor input and required mechanical advantage and speed from the gear sessions, and the depth, loads and winder distance that fix the rope angle, so sketches start informed. The brief is checked line by line against the notice, ticking safety, people and ore, scale model, lift demonstration, budget and presentation, because the board reads it to see whether the company understood what was asked.

questions.question: List four specifications and four constraints for the model headgear, each with its reason, and explain why each specification row also names a force or principle.
questions.expected_answer: Specifications: lifts a cage loaded to at least 300 grams up a 1 metre shaft in 10 to 20 seconds, because the loaded cage is the client's purpose and a lift that is too fast looks unsafe; carries the lift plus 1 kilogram on the sheave platform with less than 10 millimetres of sway at the top, because the sheave and rope loads act at the top; does not topple when the loaded cage swings 100 millimetres, because real cages swing; has a winder mechanical advantage of at least 25 with the drum turning the stated direction, because a small motor must lift the load slowly. Constraints: built from class-store materials with the gear kit and a 3 volt motor or crank; model material cost under the stated amount; fits a 300 by 300 millimetre base and passes through a door; built in two double periods with safe working practices. Each specification names its force or principle, mechanical advantage and drum speed for the lift, triangulation and the back-leg against the rope's pull for sway, wide anchored base for toppling, so the table becomes the Week 8 test plan and shows the board the rules came from engineering.

questions.question: Describe three genuinely different headgear ideas a team might sketch, state what each sketch must show and annotate, and explain why the team compares but does not choose this week.
questions.expected_answer: Idea one is a steel A-frame: a braced tower over the shaft with a back-leg to the winder on the base, sheave on a top beam, drum and gear train at the foot of the back-leg. Idea two is a four-legged braced tower with the winder and gearbox inside its base and the rope running up inside the frame to the sheave, needing no back-leg. Idea three is a closed box-section tower in the manner of a concrete headgear with the winder at the top directly over the shaft. Each sketch shows the whole headgear in rough three dimensions with the shaft below, the rope path from drum to sheave to cage, and the gear train as circles with tooth counts in position, annotated with the material of each member, the forces where they act, the safety features such as brake, bumper and guides, approximate dimensions and scale, plus a small base plan and a winder detail. The ideas are compared against the specification table, noting the A-frame's base space, the four-legged tower's rope fouling and the box tower's high centre of mass, but the choice waits for Week 6 when the other companies evaluate the sketches, so this week's task is to make all three clear enough for strangers to judge.
